1-5-2.blurb: Computers in the workforce, automated decision making, AI, environmental effects, censorship, monitoring, privacy, piracy, accessibility and culture.

questions.q: What is the difference between a MORAL and an ETHICAL issue?
o: Moral issues are always illegal; ethical ones are always legal
Moral relates to personal beliefs about right and wrong; ethical relates to shared principles of a group or profession
Ethical issues only apply to computers
questions.e: Morals are personal; ethics are the agreed standards of a community or profession.

questions.q: What is the 'digital divide'?
o: The gap between people who have access to digital technology and those who do not
The difference between analogue and digital signals
The gap between two computer networks
The boundary between a LAN and a WAN
questions.e: It can be caused by cost, location, age, skills or disability.

questions.q: Which is a possible benefit of computers in the workplace?
o: No human employees are ever needed
Tasks can be automated, increasing efficiency and allowing 24-hour operation
questions.e: Risks include job losses, deskilling and dependence on systems.

questions.q: Which is a possible negative effect of automation on employment?
o: Some jobs may be replaced, causing unemployment unless people are retrained
questions.e: New technology also creates new jobs, but workers may need new skills.

questions.q: A company uses an algorithm to shortlist job applicants. It was trained on past hiring data that favoured one group. What is the main ethical concern?
o: It will use too much storage
The algorithm may be biased and discriminate unfairly
questions.e: Training data can contain bias, which an AI system learns and repeats.

questions.q: Which is an ethical concern about decisions made by AI systems?
o: AI systems never make mistakes, so they cannot be questioned
It can be hard to explain how a decision was reached or to say who is accountable for a mistake
AI systems always explain every decision in plain English
AI decisions can only be made by the person who owns the computer
questions.e: Lack of transparency and accountability is a key ethical issue: should responsibility lie with the developer, the company using it, or the user?

questions.q: Which is an environmental concern about digital technology?
o: Digital technology always reduces energy use
Large amounts of energy are used by data centres and devices, and e-waste is hard to dispose of
questions.e: Positives: remote working can reduce travel; smart systems can improve efficiency.

questions.q: Which is an argument FOR internet censorship?
o: It can protect children from harmful content
It reduces the need for laws
questions.e: Arguments against: it restricts freedom of speech and who decides what is censored?

questions.q: Which is an argument AGAINST internet censorship?
o: It is easy to apply fairly
It can restrict freedom of speech and access to information
questions.e: Censorship raises questions about who decides what is acceptable.

questions.q: A company uses CCTV and software to monitor employees' computer use. Which is the main concern for employees?
questions.e: Benefits for employers include security, productivity and protecting data.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of analysing customers' personal data?
o: Organisations can offer personalised, targeted products and services
questions.e: Concerns: privacy, data security and how the data might be sold or misused.

questions.q: What is meant by 'piracy' in the context of digital content?
o: Illegally copying or distributing copyrighted material
questions.e: Piracy harms creators' income and is illegal under the CDPA.

questions.q: Which law makes it illegal to send indecent or offensive messages online?
questions.e: Online communication can also lead to bullying and harassment.

questions.q: Which of these helps to make a website ACCESSIBLE to people with visual impairments?
o: Using only images with no text
Alternative text for images and good colour contrast
questions.e: Other measures: transcripts or captions for audio and video, clear navigation, and adjustable text size. The Equality Act 2010 requires services not to discriminate.

questions.q: Why should designers of an international website think about colour choices?
o: All cultures interpret colours the same
Colours can have different meanings in different cultures
Colours cannot be used on websites
questions.e: E.g. white is associated with purity in some cultures and mourning in others.

questions.q: Why is Unicode recommended for international websites?
o: It can represent the characters of many different languages
It makes files smaller than any other encoding
questions.e: A limited character set such as ASCII cannot display many languages.

questions.q: Describe two ethical issues that arise from the use of automated decision-making (e.g. algorithms to approve loans or shortlist job applicants).

pts.p: The algorithm may be biased / discriminate (e.g. because of biased training data)
It may treat people unfairly or make mistakes with no human to review or challenge
It is difficult to know who is accountable / decisions can be hard to explain (lack of transparency)
It can lead to loss of jobs / de-humanises decisions / uses large amounts of personal data (privacy)

questions.model: One issue is bias: the algorithm may discriminate unfairly if it was trained on biased data, so some groups could be treated less favourably. Another is accountability and transparency: it can be hard to know who is responsible if the system makes a wrong decision, and people may be unable to understand or challenge a decision made without any human review. There are also concerns about privacy because large amounts of personal data are used, and jobs may be lost.

questions.q: Describe three ways in which a website designer could make a website more accessible to users.

pts.p: Alternative text for images (for screen readers)
Good colour contrast / option to change colours or text size
Transcripts / captions / subtitles for audio and video
Simple, consistent layout / easy navigation / clear language
Support for different languages (e.g. Unicode) / avoid culture-specific symbols or colours
Keyboard / voice control as alternatives to a mouse

questions.model: The designer could provide alternative text for images so that screen readers can describe them, use high colour contrast and allow the text size to be changed, and provide captions or transcripts for audio and video content.

questions.q: Describe two ways in which the increased use of digital technology can affect the environment.

pts.p: Data centres and devices use large amounts of electricity (increased energy use / carbon emissions)
Manufacturing devices uses raw materials / rare minerals and causes pollution / habitat damage
E-waste: devices are discarded quickly and can release toxic substances when disposed of (often exported)
Positive effects: reduced travel (remote working), paperless offices, smart systems that save energy

questions.model: Data centres and devices use large amounts of electricity, which increases energy use and carbon emissions unless the power is renewable. Manufacturing devices uses raw materials such as rare minerals and causes pollution. Devices also have a short lifespan, so large amounts of e-waste are created, which can release toxic substances if it is not disposed of or recycled properly. On the positive side, remote working and paperless systems can reduce travel and paper use.

questions.q: A school plans to install software that monitors and filters students' internet use, and analyses browsing data to identify students who may be at risk. Discuss the legal, moral, social and ethical issues the school should consider.

pts.p: Legal: the Data Protection Act 2018 / GDPR - browsing data is personal data, must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, kept secure and not kept longer than needed
Legal: students (and parents) should be informed about what is monitored and why / consent
Legal: RIPA / rules on interception of communications and the school's duty to safeguard children
Moral / ethical: monitoring invades students' privacy and may feel like constant surveillance
Moral / ethical: it can protect students from harmful content and identify those who are at risk (safeguarding)
Social: could affect trust between students and staff / stop students asking for help online
Social / ethical: filtering is a form of censorship that may block useful sites / limit freedom of access to information
Ethical: the software may be inaccurate / biased (false alarms or missing real problems)
Data security: the sensitive data collected could be hacked / misused if not kept secure
Balanced judgement: benefits vs privacy; safeguards (limit access to data, human review) to make it acceptable

questions.model: Legally, the browsing data is personal data, so the school must comply with the Data Protection Act 2018: it must process it lawfully, fairly and transparently, keep it secure, and not keep it longer than necessary. Students and parents should be told what is monitored and why, and the school has a legal duty to safeguard children. Morally and ethically, monitoring invades students' privacy and can feel like constant surveillance, but it could protect students from harmful content and identify those at risk of harm, which is a strong argument in its favour. Socially, it could damage trust between students and staff and stop students looking for help online. Filtering is a form of censorship and may block useful sites or limit access to information, and the software may be inaccurate, giving false alarms or missing real problems. The sensitive data could be hacked or misused if it is not kept secure. Overall, the benefits for safeguarding need to be balanced against privacy, and the school should use safeguards such as limiting who can see the data and having a human review any alerts.

questions.q: Discuss the social and environmental impacts of the increasing use of digital technology.

pts.p: Social: communication across the world, easier to keep in touch, share ideas and culture
Social: the digital divide - some people lack access, skills or money for technology
Social: automation / computers in the workplace can improve efficiency but replace jobs
Social: concerns about privacy, cyberbullying, addiction or less face-to-face contact
Environmental: energy use of data centres and devices (carbon emissions)
Environmental: e-waste and the extraction of raw materials
Environmental benefit: remote working / video calls / paperless reduce travel and paper
A reasoned judgement / balance of benefits and drawbacks

questions.model: Socially, digital technology allows people to communicate across the world, share ideas and keep in touch, and it creates new ways of working. However, there is a digital divide between people who have access and skills and those who do not, automation may replace jobs, and there are concerns about privacy, cyberbullying, addiction and less face-to-face contact. Environmentally, data centres and devices use a lot of energy and so contribute to carbon emissions, and manufacturing devices uses raw materials while old devices become e-waste which can be toxic if disposed of badly. On the other hand, remote working, video calls and paperless systems can reduce travel and paper use. Overall, the technology has major benefits, but the drawbacks need to be managed.

f131.notice: Original practice questions based on your F131 notes and the supplied specification. Topics 4 and 5 include extra specification-led revision to support the thinner notes. Questions and keyword marks are study guidance, not official OCR assessments.

1.title: Topic Area 1: Material properties
1.blurb: Mechanical and physical properties, tensile graphs and material testing.

questions.q: A drive shaft is twisted by a motor. Which strength is most relevant?
questions.e: Torsional strength describes resistance to twisting loads.

questions.q: Which loading condition tests compressive strength?
questions.e: Compression pushes the material together.

questions.q: A rivet resists two plates sliding in opposite directions. Which strength matters?
questions.e: Shear acts across a section as adjacent parts tend to slide.

questions.q: Which property helps a metal be drawn into a thin cable?
questions.e: Ductility is the ability to undergo plastic deformation under tensile loading.

questions.q: Which property allows sheet metal to be pressed into a panel without cracking?
questions.e: Malleability describes plastic deformation under compression.

questions.q: A machine guard must absorb an impact before fracturing. Which property is required?
questions.e: Toughness concerns energy absorbed before fracture.

questions.q: Which property describes resistance to indentation?
questions.e: Hardness is resistance to local indentation, scratching and wear.

questions.q: Which property determines how readily a metal can be cut with a tool?
questions.e: Machinability concerns the ease of machining to a suitable finish.

questions.q: What does stiffness describe?
o: Resistance to elastic deformation under load
questions.e: Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation; strength concerns failure or yielding.

questions.q: Which property matters for a turbine component under steady load at high temperature?
questions.e: Creep resistance limits time-dependent permanent deformation.

questions.q: Which is an appropriate unit for tensile strength?
questions.e: Strength as a stress is force divided by area, measured in Pa; applied load is measured in N.

questions.q: How is density defined?
questions.e: Density is commonly measured in kg/m³.

questions.q: Which physical property supports using copper in electrical cables?
questions.e: Conductivity permits current flow; copper is also ductile enough to form wire.

questions.q: A pan base should distribute heat quickly. Which property helps?
questions.e: Thermal conductivity measures how readily heat flows through a material.

questions.q: Which physical property describes size change when temperature rises?
questions.e: Thermal expansivity concerns dimensional change with temperature.

questions.q: Hardenability describes a steel’s ability to do what?
o: Develop hardness to a depth during heat treatment
questions.e: Hardenability is not the same as hardness; it concerns response and depth of hardening.

questions.q: What does fusibility describe?
questions.e: Fusibility is relevant when selecting materials for melting and casting.

questions.q: Which test uses a swinging pendulum to break a notched specimen?
questions.e: Charpy and Izod tests assess impact toughness using the energy absorbed.

questions.q: What is recorded in a Wohler fatigue test?
o: Cycles to failure at different cyclic stress levels
questions.e: Fatigue results can be plotted as an S–N curve: stress against cycles to failure.

questions.q: What happens if a specimen is unloaded within the elastic region?
o: It returns approximately to its original length
questions.e: Elastic deformation is recoverable when the load is removed.

questions.q: What is the limit of proportionality on a load–extension graph?
o: The point beyond which load and extension are no longer proportional
questions.e: Beyond this point the straight-line proportional relationship ends; it need not be exactly the yield point.

questions.q: Which feature indicates the beginning of appreciable permanent deformation in a ductile metal?
questions.e: Yielding marks plastic deformation; unloading leaves permanent extension.

questions.q: What is ultimate tensile strength?
o: The maximum engineering tensile stress reached
questions.e: UTS is the highest engineering stress in the tensile test.

questions.q: What is necking in a tensile specimen?
o: Local reduction in cross-sectional area before fracture
questions.e: Necking localises plastic deformation and commonly precedes ductile fracture.

questions.q: Which behaviour is typical of a brittle ceramic in tension?
o: Little plastic extension before sudden fracture
A long plastic region like mild steel
questions.e: Ceramics usually show limited tensile ductility and fail abruptly.

questions.q: Why may a fibre composite have different tensile responses in different directions?
o: The matrix cannot carry any load
Its reinforcement is aligned in particular directions
Its mass changes with test direction
questions.e: Fibre alignment creates anisotropy: properties depend on direction.

questions.q: Distinguish strength, stiffness and toughness when selecting a protective machine frame.

pts.p: Strength is resistance to yielding or failure under load.
Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation.
Toughness is the ability to absorb energy before fracture.

questions.model: Strength prevents failure under load. Stiffness limits elastic deformation so the frame holds its shape. Toughness allows it to absorb impact energy before fracture.

questions.q: Describe how a tensile test is carried out and identify two useful features of the load–extension graph.

pts.p: Clamp a specimen in the testing machine.
Increase tensile load and measure extension.
Identify yielding or the start of plastic deformation.
Identify maximum load or ultimate tensile strength.
Identify necking or fracture.

questions.model: Clamp a standard specimen between the grips. Apply an increasing tensile load while measuring extension. Plot load against extension to identify yielding, the maximum load associated with ultimate tensile strength, necking and fracture.

questions.q: Explain why an impact test is more useful than a hardness test for assessing a crash barrier.

pts.p: An impact test measures energy absorbed.
The barrier must resist fracture during a collision.
Hardness measures resistance to indentation, not impact energy.

questions.model: An impact test measures the energy absorbed when a specimen fractures. A barrier must absorb collision energy without brittle fracture. Hardness instead concerns resistance to indentation and does not directly measure impact toughness.

questions.q: Compare the tensile behaviour of a ductile metal and a brittle ceramic, and relate it to their suitability for an impact-loaded component.

pts.p: Both initially show elastic behaviour.
A ductile metal yields and plastically deforms.
The metal may neck before fracture.
A brittle ceramic has little plastic deformation.
The metal can absorb more energy before fracture.
Ceramic failure can occur suddenly.
A tough metal is usually preferable for impact loading.

questions.model: Both materials initially deform elastically. A ductile metal then yields and undergoes substantial plastic deformation, often with necking before fracture. This lets it absorb energy and provide warning through deformation. A brittle ceramic normally has little plastic deformation and can fracture suddenly in tension. For an impact-loaded component, a tough metal is usually preferable because it absorbs collision energy; the ceramic may still be useful where hardness or heat resistance dominates the requirements.

2.title: Topic Area 2: Types of material
2.blurb: Metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, modern materials, semiconductors and smart materials.

questions.q: Which statement defines a ferrous metal?
questions.e: Ferrous metals contain iron; stainless steel is a ferrous alloy even though some grades are non-magnetic.

questions.q: Why can an alloy be harder than its pure base metal?
o: Different-sized atoms impede movement in the lattice
All atoms become the same size
questions.e: Solute atoms distort the lattice and can hinder dislocation movement.

questions.q: Which material suits a low-cost pressed vehicle body panel?
questions.e: Low carbon steel is formable, ductile and relatively economical.

questions.q: Why is cast iron suitable for many machine bases?
o: Good compressive strength and vibration damping
questions.e: Cast iron can give rigid, vibration-damping cast shapes, but its brittleness limits tensile impact use.

questions.q: Which steel is typically selected for a wear-resistant cutting edge?
questions.e: High carbon steel can be hardened for wear resistance, at the cost of ductility.

questions.q: Why is stainless steel useful for kitchen equipment?
o: A chromium-rich passive film improves corrosion resistance
It is always the cheapest metal
questions.e: Stainless steels contain chromium which forms a protective passive oxide film.

questions.q: Why is medium carbon steel often used for shafts and gears?
o: It offers strength and responds to heat treatment
questions.e: Medium carbon steel offers a useful strength, toughness and heat-treatment balance.

questions.q: What is a common benefit of aluminium alloys in transport?
o: They always exceed steel in stiffness
questions.e: Aluminium alloys combine low density with useful strength; strength depends on alloy and processing.

questions.q: Which pairing of non-ferrous metal and application is most suitable?
o: Zinc for a high-temperature turbine blade
questions.e: Copper offers high conductivity and useful ductility.

questions.q: Why can titanium be attractive for aerospace components?
o: It is easy to cast without controls
High specific strength and corrosion resistance
questions.e: Titanium combines high strength relative to weight with corrosion resistance, but costs and processing can be drawbacks.

questions.q: Brass is chiefly an alloy of which elements?
questions.e: Brass is a copper–zinc alloy used in fittings and other formed or machined components.

questions.q: Why is nickel used in many high-temperature alloys?
o: It can support heat and corrosion resistance
questions.e: Nickel-based alloys are used where high-temperature performance is needed.

questions.q: Which statement about lithium is correct?
o: It is very low density but reactive
It is a strong structural steel
questions.e: Lithium is a low-density, reactive non-ferrous metal and is used in battery technologies.

questions.q: Which supply form is most appropriate for pressing a thin metal panel?
questions.e: Sheet is appropriate stock for forming thin panels; bar and billet serve different processes.

questions.q: Which bonding model describes a metal?
o: Separate neutral atoms with no attraction
Positive ion cores in a sea of delocalised electrons
Chains joined only by weak intermolecular forces
questions.e: Metallic bonding supports properties such as electrical conduction and plastic deformation.

questions.q: Why can a thermoplastic be softened again after forming?
o: Its covalent chain bonds must all be broken
Its chains are not permanently cross-linked into a rigid network
questions.e: Heating permits chain movement as intermolecular constraints weaken; the polymer must not be overheated into degradation.

questions.q: What forms when a thermosetting resin cures?
questions.e: Permanent cross-links prevent a cured thermoset from simply melting and being reshaped.

questions.q: Which thermoplastic is often used for transparent impact-resistant safety lenses?
questions.e: Polycarbonate offers transparency and impact resistance; scratch resistance may need a coating.

questions.q: Which material is commonly used for tough moulded toy bricks?
questions.e: ABS combines toughness and mouldability for durable moulded parts.

questions.q: Which polymer is frequently selected for food containers because of its chemical resistance?
questions.e: PP has useful chemical resistance and is commonly moulded into containers.

questions.q: Which statement about PLA is most accurate?
o: It may biodegrade under suitable controlled conditions
It always degrades quickly in the sea
questions.e: PLA is often made from renewable feedstocks, but biodegradation depends on specific conditions.

questions.q: Which material is a tough, low-cost thermoplastic used in packaging and housings?
questions.e: High impact polystyrene is a modified thermoplastic with improved impact performance.

questions.q: Which pairing uses a thermosetting polymer appropriately?
o: ABS for a permanent cross-linked adhesive
Melamine formaldehyde for a hard decorative surface
PLA for a cured resin boat matrix
questions.e: Melamine formaldehyde provides a hard, durable surface; application limits still matter.

questions.q: Which set contains only thermosetting polymers?
o: Urea formaldehyde, phenol formaldehyde and epoxy
questions.e: These resins form cross-linked structures during curing. Polyester resin is also thermosetting.

questions.q: What role does polyester resin commonly have in a GRP boat hull?
o: The matrix that binds and supports the glass fibres
questions.e: Polyester resin can act as the cured matrix in glass reinforced polymer.

questions.q: Which feature makes tungsten carbide useful in cutting tools?
o: Ability to soften like a thermoplastic
Very high hardness and wear resistance
questions.e: Carbide tooling resists wear at the cutting edge but must be protected from unsuitable impact loading.

questions.q: Why might silicon carbide be chosen for an abrasive?
o: Its ease of stretching into wire
questions.e: Silicon carbide is a hard engineering ceramic with useful thermal and wear properties.

questions.q: Which statement describes silicate glass?
o: Usually transparent, brittle and electrically insulating
questions.e: Glass can provide transparency and insulation, but brittle fracture is a key limitation.

questions.q: What is the matrix in a fibre-reinforced polymer?
o: The material that binds, supports and transfers load to fibres
Only an empty space between fibres
The element used to dope silicon
A metal coating on every fibre
questions.e: The matrix holds reinforcement together and transfers load; the fibres provide directional reinforcement.

questions.q: Which statement distinguishes a composite from an alloy?
o: A composite retains distinct matrix and reinforcement phases
An alloy is always a polymer
questions.e: Composites retain distinct phases; alloys mix a metallic base with other elements.

questions.q: Why is fibre orientation important in CRP?
o: The matrix cannot bind the fibres
Strength and stiffness depend on loading direction
Carbon fibres melt at room temperature
questions.e: Aligned fibres strongly reinforce their direction; lay-up can tailor performance.

questions.q: What is graphene?
o: A foam made only of air
A single atomic layer of carbon in a hexagonal arrangement
questions.e: Graphene is a two-dimensional carbon material with useful electrical and mechanical properties.

questions.q: What is a useful feature of metal foam?
o: A cellular structure can reduce mass and absorb energy
questions.e: Metal foams contain many pores and can provide lightweight or energy-absorbing structures.

questions.q: What distinguishes a nanomaterial?
o: It always has the same properties as bulk material
At least one relevant dimension is on the nanoscale
It must be invisible in all forms
questions.e: Nanoscale structure can change properties; effects depend on the material and design.

questions.q: Doping silicon with phosphorus usually produces what?
o: An electrically neutral insulator with no carriers
N-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
P-type with holes as majority carriers
questions.e: Phosphorus donates an extra electron. N-type refers to majority carriers, not a net negative charge of the whole material.

questions.q: Doping silicon with boron usually produces what?
o: P-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
questions.e: Boron is an acceptor dopant. The bulk semiconductor remains electrically neutral overall.

questions.q: Which pair lists another donor and acceptor respectively for silicon?
questions.e: Antimony has five valence electrons and is a donor; aluminium has three and is an acceptor.

questions.q: What creates the depletion region at a p–n junction?
o: A thick polymer coating is applied
Carrier diffusion and recombination leave fixed ionised dopants
The material melts at the interface
questions.e: Initial diffusion and recombination leave a region depleted of mobile majority carriers and establish an electric field.

questions.q: Which smart material can return to a remembered shape on heating?
questions.e: SMA undergoes a reversible structural transformation that enables shape recovery.

questions.q: Which smart material suits a temperature-sensitive colour indicator?
questions.e: Thermochromic materials change colour with temperature.

questions.q: Which smart material can darken a lens in response to light?
questions.e: Photochromic pigments respond to light intensity or UV exposure.

questions.q: A lighter generates a spark when a crystal is struck. Which effect is used?
questions.e: Mechanical stress can generate electrical charge in a piezoelectric crystal.

questions.q: What happens to QTC electrical resistance when compressed?
o: It can fall greatly, allowing more current
questions.e: Quantum tunnelling composites can be used in pressure sensors because resistance changes with compression.

questions.q: Explain why alloying a pure metal can increase its strength.

pts.p: Pure metal atoms form a relatively regular lattice.
Different-sized solute atoms distort the lattice.
This hinders dislocation movement or sliding.

questions.model: A pure metal has a relatively regular lattice. Adding different-sized solute atoms distorts this lattice. This hinders dislocation movement and makes plastic deformation more difficult, which can increase strength.

questions.q: Explain the structural difference between thermoplastics and thermosets and its effect on reheating.

pts.p: Thermoplastics contain chains without permanent cross-links between all chains.
Heating allows chain movement and softening.
Thermosets form covalent cross-links during curing.
Cured thermosets do not remelt and instead degrade on excessive heating.

questions.model: Thermoplastics contain polymer chains whose intermolecular forces allow chain movement on heating, so they soften and can be reshaped. Thermosets develop permanent covalent cross-links during curing. Their network prevents remelting; excessive heating causes degradation rather than useful reshaping.

questions.q: Explain how donor and acceptor dopants affect silicon.

pts.p: A donor such as phosphorus provides an extra electron.
N-type has electrons as majority carriers.
An acceptor such as boron creates a hole.
P-type has holes as majority carriers.

questions.model: Phosphorus is a donor with an extra valence electron, producing n-type silicon with electrons as majority carriers. Boron is an acceptor that creates a hole, producing p-type silicon with holes as majority carriers. Neither label means the whole material has a net electrical charge.

questions.q: Compare aluminium alloy and carbon reinforced polymer for a lightweight cycle frame. Make a justified choice.

pts.p: Both can reduce mass compared with common steel frames.
CRP offers high strength along aligned fibres.
Composite properties are directional.
Aluminium is easier to recycle through remelting.
CRP can be difficult to repair or recycle.
Cost and manufacture influence the decision.
A justified choice relates to performance needs.

questions.model: Both materials can reduce frame mass compared with typical steel. CRP offers high specific strength and stiffness along its fibres, but its directional properties require a carefully designed lay-up. Damage may be difficult to inspect or repair and recycling is challenging. Aluminium alloys offer useful strength at low mass and can be remelted for recycling, though joints and fatigue still need attention. Manufacturing cost also matters. I would choose aluminium for an affordable everyday frame because manufacture and recycling are more straightforward; a performance racing frame may justify the higher cost of CRP.

questions.q: Which material is a compound semiconductor made from two elements?
questions.e: Gallium arsenide combines gallium and arsenic; silicon and germanium are elemental semiconductor examples.

questions.q: Which element is another commonly studied semiconductor alongside silicon?
questions.e: Germanium is an elemental semiconductor; its conductivity depends on carrier behaviour and doping.

questions.q: Why can indium act as an acceptor dopant in suitable group-IV semiconductor material?
o: It always supplies two extra electrons
questions.e: A trivalent dopant can create holes in a tetravalent host; the effect depends on the host material.

questions.q: What does NPN describe in a bipolar transistor?
o: Three layers of unmodified pure metal
A p-type region between two p-type regions
A p-type base between two n-type regions
questions.e: NPN refers to emitter, base and collector doping regions, not net electrical charges of the bulk layers.

questions.q: What does PNP describe in a bipolar transistor?
o: A p-type base between two n-type regions
An n-type base between two p-type regions
questions.e: PNP has the complementary doping arrangement to NPN. Transistors are used for switching and amplification.

questions.q: Which bonding types are important in engineering ceramics?
questions.e: Strong ionic and covalent bonds contribute to ceramic hardness and high-temperature performance, while many ceramics remain brittle.

questions.q: Which application can benefit from metal foam’s ability to absorb energy?
questions.e: Cellular metal structures can deform and absorb impact energy while keeping mass relatively low.

questions.q: Why can nanostructured materials be useful in surface coatings?
o: Their small-scale structure can alter surface properties
They always remove every environmental risk
questions.e: Nanostructure can modify functions such as wettability or wear behaviour; performance depends on the material and design.

3.title: Topic Area 3: Processing and heat treatment
3.blurb: How forming, joining, polymer processing, ceramic production and heat treatment change materials.

questions.q: What temperature condition distinguishes hot working from cold working?
o: Hot working occurs above the recrystallisation temperature
Hot working always occurs above melting point
questions.e: Recrystallisation is the key reference, not an absolute temperature or the melting point.

questions.q: What is a usual effect of cold working a metal?
o: Higher strength and hardness with reduced ductility
questions.e: Work hardening increases resistance to plastic deformation but can reduce ductility.

questions.q: Why can hot working allow large deformation?
o: The metal must be a liquid
questions.e: New grains form during or after deformation at sufficiently high temperatures.

questions.q: What happens during rolling?
o: A cutting tool removes all the stock
A wire is dipped in zinc
Metal passes between rotating rolls to change its section
questions.e: Rolling uses compressive forces and can reduce sheet thickness.

questions.q: Which process shapes metal using a hammer or press?
questions.e: Forging uses compressive force and can create beneficial grain flow.

questions.q: Why can forged grain flow improve a component?
o: It can align the structure with service loads
questions.e: Favourable grain flow can improve strength and fatigue performance in relevant directions.

questions.q: What is press forming commonly used to produce?
o: Sheet-metal shapes using a punch and die
questions.e: A press forces stock into or over a die; tool design, force and formability matter.

questions.q: What distinguishes fusion welding from brazing?
o: Brazing always melts all parent material
Fusion welding melts the parent material locally
questions.e: Fusion welding joins through local parent-metal melting; brazing melts the filler without melting the parent metal.

questions.q: Why must a weld heat-affected zone be considered?
o: Heating and cooling can change local microstructure and properties
It is always stronger than all parent metal
questions.e: The heat-affected zone can change hardness, toughness and residual stress.

questions.q: What is the key shaping step in casting?
o: Pour molten material into a mould and let it solidify
Force cold powder through a wire die
Cut stock on a lathe only
questions.e: Casting relies on solidification in a mould; cooling controls structure and defects.

questions.q: Which casting defect can reduce component strength?
questions.e: Voids reduce effective load-bearing area and can initiate cracks.

questions.q: Which description best fits turning?
o: A cutting tool removes material from rotating stock
questions.e: Turning is a subtractive lathe process, unlike forming or casting.

questions.q: What happens first in a typical thermoplastic injection moulding cycle?
o: Feed granules into a heated barrel
questions.e: Granules are fed and melted, then injected under pressure into a mould, cooled and ejected.

questions.q: Why can an injection moulded part shrink or warp?
o: The mould removes all heat instantly
Cooling contraction and uneven residual stresses
questions.e: Cooling rates, shrinkage and residual stresses affect dimensions and shape.

questions.q: Which feature can form where two molten polymer flow fronts meet?
o: A weld line that may be mechanically weaker
questions.e: Flow-front joining can create a weld line; processing and tooling should manage it.

questions.q: What does curing do to a thermosetting resin?
o: Turns all chains into separate gases immediately
questions.e: Curing builds the polymer network and determines final properties.

questions.q: Why is under-curing a resin a problem?
o: Insufficient cross-linking can reduce stiffness and stability
questions.e: An under-cured matrix may be weaker and less thermally or dimensionally stable.

questions.q: What is a principal effect of sintering ceramic powder?
o: Particles bond and porosity can decrease
questions.e: Heat promotes particle bonding and densification; full bulk melting is not required.

questions.q: What is a purpose of firing a ceramic body?
o: Develop a durable body through heat-driven physical and chemical changes
questions.e: Firing can remove binders and develop structure, strength and density.

questions.q: What is the matrix role during composite lay-up?
o: Replace every fibre with an air bubble
Wet, bind and support the reinforcement before curing
questions.e: Lay-up combines oriented reinforcement and resin; curing fixes the structure.

questions.q: Why might a lay-up use layers with different fibre directions?
o: To resist loads in more than one direction
To ensure identical mass in every part
questions.e: Different orientations tailor directional strength and stiffness to service loads.

questions.q: Which treatment aims to give a hard outer layer and a tougher core?
questions.e: Case hardening provides a wear-resistant case while retaining core toughness.

questions.q: Rapidly cooling suitably heated carbon steel can form which hard structure?
questions.e: Quench hardening can form martensite, increasing hardness but also brittleness and residual stress.

questions.q: Why is quenched steel often tempered afterwards?
o: To reduce brittleness and improve toughness
questions.e: Tempering reheats below the critical transformation temperature and balances hardness with toughness.

questions.q: How is normalising steel typically completed after suitable heating?
o: Immediate cooling in liquid nitrogen only
questions.e: Normalising promotes a refined, more uniform structure through heating and air cooling.

questions.q: Why might an aluminium alloy be annealed before further forming?
o: To restore ductility and reduce work-hardening effects
To form a steel martensite case
questions.e: Annealing softens work-hardened material and improves formability.

questions.q: What is the purpose of precipitation hardening in suitable aluminium alloys?
o: The metal becomes non-crystalline glass in every case
questions.e: Solution treatment, quenching and ageing develop strengthening precipitates.

questions.q: Explain how cold working changes a metal’s structure and properties.

pts.p: Plastic deformation increases dislocation density.
Dislocations hinder further movement.
Strength rises while ductility falls.

questions.model: Cold working plastically deforms the metal and increases dislocation density. Interactions between dislocations hinder further movement, causing work hardening. Strength and hardness increase but ductility decreases.

questions.q: Describe the main stages of thermoplastic injection moulding.

pts.p: Feed polymer granules into a heated barrel.
Melt the polymer.
Inject molten polymer into the mould under pressure.
Cool, solidify and eject the part.

questions.model: Feed polymer granules into a heated barrel where a screw moves and melts the polymer. Inject the molten material into a closed mould under pressure. Allow it to cool and solidify, then open the mould and eject the part.

questions.q: Explain why a steel cutting tool might be quenched and then tempered.

pts.p: Quenching forms a hard structure such as martensite.
Hardness improves wear resistance.
Quenching may cause brittleness or residual stress.
Tempering improves toughness at some cost in hardness.

questions.model: Quenching suitably heated steel can form hard martensite, improving wear resistance at the cutting edge. However, the quenched steel may be brittle and contain residual stress. Tempering reduces brittleness and improves toughness, with a controlled reduction in hardness.

questions.q: A manufacturer is choosing between a forged steel part and a cast steel part for a heavily loaded lever. Compare their manufacture, structure and likely performance.

pts.p: Forging shapes solid metal using compressive force.
Casting solidifies molten metal in a mould.
Forging can align grain flow with loads.
Casting can produce complex shapes.
Porosity in a casting can initiate failure.
Tooling, finish or machining costs matter.
Recommendation links to load or performance.

questions.model: Forging uses compressive force to shape solid metal and can align grain flow with the lever’s main load paths. This can support strength and fatigue performance. Casting pours molten steel into a mould and can produce complex shapes, but solidification defects such as porosity can initiate cracks. Tooling, finishing and machining costs differ and must be considered alongside production volume. I would recommend a well-designed forging for the heavily loaded lever where fatigue resistance matters, while checking the geometry, heat treatment and cost requirements rather than assuming all forged parts are automatically superior.

questions.q: Why is process temperature important when selecting a heat treatment?
o: Every treatment uses the same temperature
Only paint colour changes with temperature
It has no effect on microstructure
It controls which structural transformations can occur
questions.e: Correct heating and cooling depend on the alloy, its transformation temperatures and the required properties; one universal temperature is not appropriate.

4.title: Topic Area 4: Failure mechanisms and prevention
4.blurb: Overstress, fracture, fatigue, creep, erosion, corrosion and practical prevention methods. Specification supplements included.

questions.q: A bracket carries a load far above its design limit and permanently bends. Which mechanism is most likely?
questions.e: An excessive stress can cause yielding, excessive deformation or fracture.

questions.q: What characterises brittle fracture?
o: Sudden fracture with little plastic deformation
questions.e: Brittle fracture can give little warning and is sensitive to cracks and stress concentration.

questions.q: A shaft breaks after many rotating load cycles below yield strength. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.e: Fatigue damage accumulates under cyclic loading even when stress is below yield strength.

questions.q: Which feature is most likely to initiate a fatigue crack?
o: A sharp internal corner or notch
questions.e: Notches, keyways, holes and scratches can concentrate stress.

questions.q: Which change generally reduces fatigue risk at a shoulder?
questions.e: A smooth gradual transition reduces local stress concentration.

questions.q: What distinguishes creep from fatigue?
o: Creep only occurs in cold water
Creep is time-dependent deformation under sustained load
questions.e: Creep is often important at elevated temperature under sustained stress; fatigue involves repeated loading.

questions.q: How does the strain rate behave during primary creep?
o: It alternates with each electrical pulse
questions.e: Initial creep slows as strain-hardening effects develop.

questions.q: How does the strain rate behave during secondary creep?
o: It increases without limit from the start
It is defined by total fracture
questions.e: Secondary creep has an approximately constant rate and often occupies much of service life.

questions.q: What occurs during tertiary creep?
o: The deformation rate accelerates towards rupture
The material fully returns to its original shape
The temperature must fall to zero
questions.e: Damage and loss of effective section accelerate deformation and lead towards rupture.

questions.q: Which operating change can reduce creep risk?
questions.e: Creep depends strongly on temperature and stress; reducing either can extend life.

questions.q: A slurry pipe becomes thinner where fast-moving particles strike it. What mechanism is involved?
questions.e: Moving particles or fluid can remove surface material and thin the wall.

questions.q: Why can constrained thermal expansion cause failure?
o: Heating always reduces stress to zero
Prevented expansion creates stress and may cause buckling
questions.e: Free expansion may be harmless; restraint converts thermal strain into stress.

questions.q: What is a likely consequence of repeated heating and cooling?
o: Formation of a new virgin resource
questions.e: Thermal cycling can repeatedly strain the material or its joints.

questions.q: What is corrosion?
o: Material degradation through chemical or electrochemical interaction with the environment
An increase in all useful dimensions
questions.e: Corrosion can reduce thickness, alter surfaces and initiate failure.

questions.q: Why can pitting be dangerous even when overall mass loss is small?
o: Deep local cavities weaken sections and concentrate stress
questions.e: Local pits can penetrate thin walls and act as crack initiators.

questions.q: Which conditions contribute to stress corrosion cracking?
o: A perfect vacuum with no stress in every case
Only compressive loading in every alloy
A susceptible material, tensile stress and a corrosive environment
questions.e: SCC requires a relevant combination of material, tensile stress and environment.

questions.q: What is the main protection provided by intact paint?
o: It acts as a barrier to moisture and oxygen
It always sacrifices itself electrochemically like zinc
It hardens the entire metal core
It eliminates all need for maintenance
questions.e: Paint isolates the metal surface, but damage can expose the substrate.

questions.q: What is a limitation of powder or polymer coatings?
o: Damage can expose the substrate and allow corrosion
questions.e: Coatings need suitable application and inspection; damage reduces barrier protection.

questions.q: How is electroplating applied?
o: A ceramic is fired without a metal substrate
Every atom is replaced with silicon
A metal layer is deposited using an electrical process
Steel is melted inside polymer granules
questions.e: Electroplating can improve surface properties. Its corrosion protection depends on metal choice and coating continuity.

questions.q: What does galvanising usually apply to steel?
questions.e: Zinc provides a barrier and can also act sacrificially in suitable conditions.

questions.q: Why can galvanised steel remain protected around a small scratch?
o: The scratch instantly fills with new steel
Zinc is always less reactive than iron
questions.e: Zinc can sacrifice itself to protect steel, but the coating is consumed over time.

questions.q: What happens in sacrificial-anode cathodic protection?
o: The method requires no conductive path
A more reactive connected metal corrodes instead of the protected component
The protected steel must become the anode
questions.e: The protected component is made the cathode. Electrical connection and a suitable electrolyte are needed.

questions.q: What maintenance is needed for a sacrificial-anode system?
o: Make the anode less reactive than steel
Polish the protected steel once and never check it
questions.e: Anodes are consumed and must remain connected and sufficiently available.

questions.q: Which statement about impressed-current cathodic protection is correct?
o: It is identical to a paint barrier
It requires the component to be isolated from the circuit
It uses an external electrical supply and needs monitoring
questions.e: Impressed current can protect large structures but relies on power and controlled operation.

questions.q: Which surface change generally reduces fatigue crack initiation?
o: Remove scratches and improve the surface finish
questions.e: A smoother finish reduces surface stress raisers. Suitable surface treatments can further improve service performance.

questions.q: Why might surface hardening help a loaded part?
o: It can improve wear resistance and, with suitable residual stress, fatigue performance
It guarantees no failure at any load
It removes all need for a tough core
questions.e: Treatment must match material and loading; a hard surface alone is not a universal cure.

questions.q: Which design strategy reduces stress raisers?
o: Use consistent sections and smooth transitions where practical
questions.e: Geometry and load paths matter alongside material selection and processing.

questions.q: Explain how cyclic loading and a sharp keyway can cause fatigue failure in a shaft.

pts.p: Repeated cyclic stress can cause damage below yield strength.
A keyway acts as a stress raiser.
A crack initiates and grows with cycles.
The remaining section eventually fractures.

questions.model: Cyclic loading can cause fatigue even below yield strength. A sharp keyway concentrates stress and can initiate a crack. The crack grows with successive cycles until the remaining load-bearing section is too small, leading to final fracture.

questions.q: Describe the three stages of creep in a hot loaded component.

pts.p: Primary creep has a decreasing strain rate.
Secondary creep has an approximately constant rate.
Tertiary creep accelerates towards rupture.

questions.model: In primary creep the strain rate decreases. Secondary creep proceeds at an approximately constant strain rate. In tertiary creep damage and loss of effective section accelerate deformation towards rupture.

questions.q: Compare paint and galvanising for protecting an outdoor steel railing.

pts.p: Paint provides a barrier.
Scratches in paint expose steel.
Galvanising adds a zinc coating.
Zinc can protect sacrificially but is consumed.
Maintenance or recoating is required.

questions.model: Intact paint provides a barrier to water and oxygen, but scratches expose the steel and require repair. Galvanising coats the steel with zinc, which acts as a barrier and can corrode sacrificially near small scratches. Zinc is consumed over time, so neither method removes the need for inspection and maintenance.

questions.q: Explain why a scratched plated component may corrode, and why coating material choice matters.

pts.p: A scratch can expose the substrate.
A barrier coating works best when continuous.
Sacrificial protection depends on relative reactivity.

questions.model: A scratch exposes the substrate to the environment. A continuous barrier coating protects effectively, but a damaged coating may not. Whether the coating can protect sacrificially depends on its reactivity relative to the substrate; not every electroplated metal protects steel like zinc.

questions.q: A hot pump shaft operates in corrosive fluid with repeated loads. Recommend changes to reduce failure, explaining their benefits and limits.

pts.p: Repeated loads create fatigue risk.
Use smoother geometry to reduce stress concentration.
Reduce operating temperature or sustained stress to limit creep.
Select corrosion-resistant material or a suitable coating.
Inspect damage and maintain protection.
Protection has limitations in the operating environment.
Changes must retain required pump performance.

questions.model: Repeated shaft loads can cause fatigue, particularly at sharp section changes, so I would add fillets and improve the surface finish to reduce stress concentration. Where sustained stress and temperature are high enough for creep, lower the operating temperature or load if pump performance allows it. A corrosion-resistant material or suitable coating can limit attack and pitting, but coating damage may expose the shaft. I would inspect for cracks, pits and coating damage and maintain the protection. Any change must be checked against fluid compatibility, flow and pressure requirements, because a treatment that works in one environment may be unsuitable in another.

5.title: Topic Area 5: Sustainable materials and practices
5.blurb: Circular economy, finite resources, all six Rs, design efficiency and sorting for recycling. Specification supplements included.

questions.q: What is a central aim of a circular economy?
o: Keep products and materials in useful circulation
Send all products directly to landfill
questions.e: Circular design seeks to avoid waste and preserve value through maintenance, repair, reuse and recycling.

questions.q: Which approach is most consistent with circular design?
o: A product designed for repair and eventual material recovery
A sealed product that cannot be dismantled
An unnecessarily mixed material that cannot be separated
questions.e: Design choices influence whether materials and components remain useful.

questions.q: Why does petroleum use for many virgin polymers raise sustainability concerns?
o: It consumes a finite resource and has environmental impacts
questions.e: Resource extraction and processing affect the environment; the feedstock is finite.

questions.q: Why can virgin metal production have a high environmental impact?
o: Mining and energy-intensive extraction and processing
questions.e: Ore extraction, refining and processing can consume energy and produce emissions or waste.

questions.q: Why can ceramic production use substantial energy?
o: All ceramics are formed without heat
questions.e: Firing and other thermal processing contribute to the production footprint.

questions.q: Which set matches the six Rs in the supplied F131 specification?
o: Reduce, Remove, Repeat, Recycle, Refit, Repair
Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Recycle, Reuse, Repair
Rethink, Replace, Reduce, Recycle, Reuse, Repair
Refuse, Rebuild, Repaint, Recycle, Reuse, Repair
questions.e: The supplied specification explicitly lists these six Rs.

questions.q: A designer asks whether a powered product is necessary at all. Which R is this?
questions.e: Rethink questions the need, function or design approach before making the product.

questions.q: A manufacturer avoids an unnecessary hazardous finishing treatment. Which R fits best?
questions.e: Refuse means avoiding unnecessary or unsuitable resource use or processes.

questions.q: A part is redesigned to use less material while retaining safe strength. Which R is most relevant?
questions.e: Reduce cuts resource consumption without compromising required function or safety.

questions.q: A used housing is cleaned and used again without converting it to raw material. Which R is this?
questions.e: Reuse preserves the product or component rather than reprocessing it into material.

questions.q: A worn bearing is replaced so a machine can remain in service. Which R applies?
questions.e: Repair restores function and can extend the service life.

questions.q: Used aluminium is remelted and formed into new products. Which R applies?
questions.e: Recycling processes recovered material into feedstock for new products.

questions.q: How can design for manufacture reduce resource use?
o: Simplify parts and reduce manufacturing waste
Require more machining scrap without a reason
questions.e: Efficient geometry, processes and tolerances can reduce waste and energy use.

questions.q: Why can modular construction support sustainability?
o: Faulty modules can be replaced while useful parts remain
questions.e: Modularity can simplify repair, upgrading and component reuse.

questions.q: Why might a product use fasteners instead of permanent adhesive at an accessible joint?
o: To aid disassembly and material separation
questions.e: Reversible joints can improve repair and end-of-life separation where mechanically suitable.

questions.q: What information can a plastic identification marking provide?
o: A guarantee that every local facility accepts it
The polymer type to support sorting
questions.e: Identification helps sorting but does not guarantee local recyclability or contamination-free material.

questions.q: Which material can an ordinary magnet most readily separate from mixed scrap?
o: All grades of stainless steel without exception
questions.e: Magnetic sorting can recover ferromagnetic metals, but not every ferrous alloy responds equally.

questions.q: Why cannot magnetic sorting alone separate every non-ferrous metal?
o: Many non-ferrous metals are not attracted by an ordinary magnet
They all melt at room temperature
questions.e: Additional methods are needed to identify or sort non-ferrous metals.

questions.q: Why is mixing incompatible polymer types a recycling problem?
o: It eliminates the need for sorting
It converts the waste into pure steel
It can reduce the quality and predictable properties of the recycled material
questions.e: Separation and contamination control help maintain suitable recycled feedstock quality.

questions.q: Which is a realistic application for suitable recycled polymer?
o: Every safety-critical part with no testing
Any food-contact product without checking rules
A replacement for all turbine alloys
A non-critical housing after property checks
questions.e: Suitability depends on material quality, function, traceability and required approvals.

questions.q: When may virgin material be necessary?
o: When a required specification cannot be met by available recycled feedstock
For every engineering product regardless of quality
Only when a product is decorative
questions.e: Some purity, traceability or performance requirements cannot be met by the available recovered material; the decision is application-specific.

questions.q: Which statement about recycled metal in safety-critical use is most accurate?
o: It can be used if composition, quality and traceability meet the required specification
It always meets every specification without testing
questions.e: Recycled origin alone does not determine suitability; verified material requirements matter.

questions.q: Why should engineers compare whole-life impacts?
o: Only the colour of packaging matters
Use, maintenance and end-of-life can change the overall result
questions.e: A lower production footprint may not give the best whole-life outcome if service life or energy use is worse.

questions.q: Which consequence can follow from unsustainable production?
o: Resource depletion, pollution and increased waste
questions.e: Unsustainable practices can harm resource availability and environmental quality.

questions.q: Why is replacing a durable material with a weaker lightweight material not automatically sustainable?
o: Shorter service life or failures may outweigh the material saving
questions.e: Resource savings must be balanced with safe performance, life, repairability and disposal.

questions.q: Why can closed-loop collection improve material recovery?
o: Known material streams help control contamination and quality
It needs no sorting or checks
questions.e: Collecting known material streams supports traceability and recovery but still requires processing and checks.

questions.q: Distinguish reuse, repair and recycling using an engineering example for each.

pts.p: Reuse uses a component again without material reprocessing.
Repair restores function by fixing damage.
Recycling processes recovered material into new feedstock.

questions.model: Reuse could mean using a sound motor again in another machine. Repair could mean replacing a failed bearing to restore the machine’s function. Recycling could mean remelting a worn aluminium housing to produce new material feedstock.

questions.q: Suggest four design changes that reduce waste and extend the life of an electronic product.

pts.p: Provide access for repair.
Use replaceable or modular components.
Use efficient geometry to reduce material waste.
Use separable materials or reversible joints.
Avoid unnecessary finishes or material types.

questions.model: Make repair points accessible and use replaceable modular components. Reduce unnecessary material through efficient geometry while keeping safe performance. Use reversible joints so different materials can be separated for recovery, and avoid unnecessary finishes that complicate recycling.

questions.q: Explain how plastic identification markings and magnetic sorting support recycling, including one limitation of each.

pts.p: Plastic markings identify polymer type.
Identification does not guarantee local recyclability.
Magnets separate ferromagnetic metals.
Magnets cannot recover every metal type.

questions.model: Plastic identification markings show the polymer type, helping compatible materials be sorted together, but a code does not guarantee local recycling facilities accept it. Magnets can recover ferromagnetic steel from mixed waste, but cannot attract every metal, including most non-ferrous metals and some stainless steels.

questions.q: Explain why recycled material must be checked before being used in a safety-critical component.

pts.p: Composition or properties may vary.
Contamination or defects can affect performance.
Quality and traceability must meet the component specification.

questions.model: Recovered material can have variable composition and properties. Contamination or defects may affect component performance. Testing, quality control and traceability must demonstrate that the feedstock meets the required specification; if available recycled material cannot meet it, virgin material may be necessary.

questions.q: A manufacturer plans to replace a disposable sealed tool with a repairable design. Evaluate its sustainability using the six Rs and whole-life considerations.

pts.p: Rethink whether the product or design is necessary.
Refuse unnecessary materials or processes.
Reduce material or energy consumption.
Reuse suitable components.
Repair extends service life.
Recycle recoverable material at end of life.
Evaluate use, transport, cost or manufacturing impacts.
Make a reasoned judgement on whole-life performance.

questions.model: Rethink whether the tool needs its current design and refuse unnecessary finishes or difficult-to-separate materials. Reduce material and energy use while preserving safe function. A repairable design lets the manufacturer reuse sound components and repair worn parts, extending service life. Recycle suitable materials at the end of life through accessible disassembly and clear identification. Extra fasteners, spare-part transport and manufacturing impacts may increase initial resource use or cost. I would favour the repairable design if its longer life and reduced replacement demand outweigh those extra impacts over the whole life of the product.
